indications: Pneumothorax needing drainage: tension after decompression, secondary pneumothorax, symptomatic primary pneumothorax after failed or declined aspiration, and pneumothorax in a ventilated patient.
Haemothorax and haemopneumothorax, typically with a large-bore drain in trauma.
Pleural infection (empyema or complicated parapneumonic effusion).
Symptomatic effusion needing drainage, and pleurodesis.
contraindications: No safe window on ultrasound for a fluid drain.
Suspected large bulla or lobar collapse mistaken for pneumothorax or effusion: CT first.
Relative: uncorrected coagulopathy or anticoagulation in an elective case, previous pleurodesis or surgery on that side (adhesions), skin infection at the site.
A post-pneumonectomy space, unless directed by the thoracic team.
preparation: Confirm the side and indication against current imaging; mark the side.
Thoracic ultrasound for every fluid drain, at the bedside, with the patient in the position of insertion.
Written consent where possible: pain, bleeding, infection, failure, organ injury and malposition.
Use a procedural safety checklist, an assistant, monitoring, oxygen and resuscitation equipment.
Premedication with analgesia; sedation only with appropriate monitoring.
positioning: Semi-recumbent with the ipsilateral arm behind the head, exposing the axilla.
Alternatively, sitting and leaning forward over a table for posterior fluid collections under ultrasound guidance.
equipment: Seldinger kit: introducer needle, guidewire, dilators and small-bore drain.
For blunt dissection: scalpel, curved blunt forceps (for example a Spencer Wells), large-bore drain without a trocar.
Local anaesthetic, sterile pack, suture for securing the drain, dressing.
Underwater seal bottle primed with sterile water, or a valved system as appropriate.
anatomy: The safe triangle: anterior border of latissimus dorsi, lateral border of pectoralis major, a horizontal line at the level of the nipple (fifth intercostal space), apex below the axilla.
The neurovascular bundle runs along the inferior border of each rib. Insert just above the upper border of the rib below.
The diaphragm rises high in expiration, especially on the right with the liver beneath; below the nipple line it may be at the insertion site.
The long thoracic nerve runs on serratus anterior behind the mid-axillary line; the intercostal vessels are tortuous posteriorly and in older patients.
criticalSafety: Stay above the rib below and within the safe triangle.
Aspirate air or fluid with the anaesthetic needle before committing to the drain. No aspirate, no drain.
Account for the guidewire after every Seldinger insertion.
Never clamp a bubbling drain; keep the bottle below the chest.
commonErrors: Inserting too low, below the nipple line, into the abdomen.
Not confirming fluid on ultrasound immediately before insertion.
Pushing the dilator or drain too deep with force, risking lung or mediastinal injury.
Securing the drain with a purse-string suture that later causes a poor scar, or with a suture that does not hold the drain.
complications: Bleeding from intercostal vessel injury, and haemothorax.
Malposition: subcutaneous, intra-fissural, intra-abdominal or intrapulmonary.
Organ injury: lung, liver, spleen, heart.
Drain displacement or blockage, especially with small-bore drains.
Infection at the site or empyema; surgical emphysema; re-expansion pulmonary oedema.
postop: Drain chart: swinging, bubbling, volume and character, recorded at least daily and hourly in haemothorax.
Flush small-bore drains per local protocol to prevent blockage.
Daily review of the need for the drain; remove when the indication has resolved.

steps.emphasis: Confirm the side against the imaging AND the examination. Wrong-side chest drains are reported every year.
A bedside procedure deserves the same pause: identity, side, indication, imaging, coagulation and allergies.
Arm behind the head opens the safe triangle and moves latissimus dorsi back.
Full aseptic technique: skin preparation, sterile gloves and gown, and a large sterile drape.
For Seldinger drains, the guidewire is seen and accounted for after the drain is in. A retained guidewire is a never event.
Document side, site, size, technique, ultrasound use, fluid character and volume, and the plan for drain management.

step.cd.site.title: Site selection with ultrasound
step.cd.site.why: Most serious drain injuries come from inserting where there is no pleural target or below the diaphragm. Ultrasound shows where the target is and where the diaphragm moves.
how: Identify the safe triangle by palpation.
For fluid, scan the site and mark it with the patient in the insertion position, noting depth to pleura and the diaphragm position through respiration.
For pneumothorax, confirm the side on imaging and choose a site in the safe triangle, usually the fourth or fifth space in the mid-axillary line.
pitfalls: Marking on one day and inserting on another.
Using a radiograph alone to choose a fluid site.

step.cd.anaesthesia.title: Local anaesthesia and confirmatory aspiration
step.cd.anaesthesia.why: Adequate local anaesthesia makes the procedure tolerable, and aspirating air or fluid with the needle confirms that the pleural space is where you think it is.
how: Infiltrate skin, then the tissues just above the upper border of the rib, down to the parietal pleura, which is the most sensitive layer.
Aspirate as you advance. Air or fluid confirms entry into the pleural space and gives the depth.
Stay within the maximum safe dose of local anaesthetic for the patient's weight.
pitfalls: Proceeding when the needle aspirates nothing.
Insufficient anaesthesia of the parietal pleura.

step.cd.seldinger.title: Seldinger technique (small-bore drain)
step.cd.seldinger.why: Small-bore drains are first line for most pneumothoraces and effusions; they are less painful and as effective. The risk lies in the dilator, which can go too deep.
how: Advance the introducer needle above the rib, aspirating, until air or fluid is obtained.
Pass the guidewire through the needle, remove the needle, and keep hold of the wire at all times.
Make a small skin nick and pass the dilator over the wire only to the depth of the pleura measured on the needle, holding it close to the skin to limit depth.
Pass the drain over the wire to the planned length, remove the wire, and connect to the drainage system.
structuresAtRisk: Mediastinum if the dilator is pushed too far
pitfalls: Losing the guidewire into the chest.
Dilating with excessive force or depth.

step.cd.blunt.title: Blunt dissection technique (large-bore drain)
step.cd.blunt.why: Large-bore drains are used for trauma haemothorax and some viscous collections. Blunt dissection into the pleura with a finger sweep confirms the space and finds adhesions before the drain goes in.
how: Make a skin incision of a size to admit a finger, parallel to the rib, over the space chosen.
Spread bluntly with curved forceps over the top of the rib below and through the intercostal muscles, then puncture the parietal pleura.
Insert a finger to confirm the pleural space and sweep for adhesions and the lung.
Guide the drain in with forceps or a finger, directed apically for air and basally for fluid, without a trocar.
pitfalls: A skin incision too small, leading to force.

step.cd.secure.title: Securing the drain and connecting the seal
step.cd.secure.why: Drain displacement is a common reason for repeat procedures. A well-anchored drain connected to a correctly primed seal is the end of the procedure, not an afterthought.
how: Anchor the drain with a strong suture, avoiding purse-string sutures that cause poor scars.
Apply a transparent dressing that allows the site to be seen; add an omental tag of tape.
Connect to an underwater seal, confirm the tube is submerged, and check for swinging and bubbling.

step.cd.confirm.title: Confirming position and function
step.cd.confirm.why: A drain that swings and drains is in the pleura; a radiograph confirms it is in the right part of it and that no complication has followed.
how: Observe swinging with respiration and bubbling or drainage.
Chest radiograph after insertion.
Control the drainage of large effusions and stop for chest tightness or cough.
pitfalls: Draining a large effusion all at once.
